paraphrase: The four accomplishments (ārādhanā) — of right faith, right knowledge, right conduct and austerity — are to be perfected together and above all at the end of life.

Death is classified as the death of the wise-among-the-wise (the omniscient), of the wise (the monk), of the wise-ignorant (the layman with vows), of the ignorant (one with right faith but no vows) and of the ignorant-among-the-ignorant (one of wrong faith).

The fast unto death is to be undertaken only when death cannot be averted, with the teacher's permission, gradually, under the care of attending ascetics (niryāpaka) who strengthen the dying one with instruction and recitation; it is ruined by fear, by longing for life or death, by desire for rewards, and by attachment.

paraphrase: The sign of renunciation is normally the natural one (autsargika-liṅga): nakedness, the plucked head and the whisk; for those with a just cause (such as a bodily defect or public shame) an exceptional sign (āpavādika-liṅga) with cloth is allowed, which may be given up at the approach of death.

paraphrase: Death is of five kinds — the 'wise-wise' death of the omniscient, the wise death of the restrained ascetic, the wise-foolish death of the layman, the foolish death of one with right view but no vows, and the foolish-foolish death of the wrong-believer; the wise death, by one of three kinds of renunciation of food, is praised.
